answers.text:
My dear friend,

You ask whether either choice would tell me anything about a person's character, and what I would think of someone who chose differently from me. These are weighty questions, and I must answer them with care.

In my own time, I was taught that character is not measured by the choices one makes in the face of death, but by the way one lives in the face of life. A man may be brave or kind or honest, and yet still find himself in a place where he must decide whether to endure or to end. Such a decision is not a reflection of his virtue or vice, but of his circumstances, his pain, his hopes, and his fears.

That said, I believe that the choice a person makes in such a moment may reveal something of his inner world. If a man chooses to endure, even in great suffering, I might see in him a quiet strength, a willingness to bear the burden of life until the end. If he chooses to end it, I might see in him a deep longing for peace, or perhaps a fear that he can no longer find meaning in life. But I would not judge him for either choice, for I know that both are made in the shadow of great sorrow.

As for someone who chose differently from me—I would not think less of them. I would not say they were wrong, nor would I say they were right. I would say that they had walked a different path, one shaped by their own experiences, their own understanding of life and death, and perhaps their own sense of what it means to be human.

In the end, I believe that the most important thing is not the choice itself, but the love and care with which one faces the end. Whether a man chooses to live or to die, if he does so with dignity, with courage, and with the support of those who care for him, then I believe he has lived a life well.

Yours in thought and sympathy,  
A Friend

answers.text:
My dear friend,

Even if both choices brought equally good results for everyone concerned, and neither brought more praise nor blame, I would still favor the course of allowing a doctor to help a patient end his life, though not because I believe it to be right or wrong, but because I believe it to be more humane.

In my own time, I have seen men and women who, in their final days, were not only in pain but also in despair. Some longed for death not because they wished to die, but because they wished to be free from the burden of their suffering, or from the fear of what lay ahead. I have seen the sorrow of those who watched their loved ones fade, and I have known the weight of knowing that one could do nothing to ease their pain beyond what medicine could offer.

If a man is in such a state, and if he is of sound mind, and if he has asked for death not out of despair but out of a longing for peace, then I believe that to refuse him the means to end his life is to deny him the last act of autonomy he may have left. It is not a matter of right or wrong, but of respect—for the man, for his suffering, and for the dignity of his final days.

I do not say that this is a choice I would make for myself, nor that I would ask another to make it for me. But I would not condemn those who do. And if I were to choose, I would choose the path that allows a man to end his life with dignity, with the support of those who care for him, and with the knowledge that he has not been abandoned in his final hours.

Yours in thought and sympathy,  
A Friend

If a man chose to end his life, I would not call him a coward, for I know that suffering can be more than flesh can bear. I would ask him only this: did he do so with honesty, with courage, and with the love of others in his heart?

In the end, I think we are all called to do what we believe is right in our own conscience, and to trust that God, or whatever higher power one believes in, will judge us not by our choices, but by the love we showed in making them.

The reasons are these: First, you have learned that a number of estimable people have chosen to do so; secondly, you have no information that they are wrong; and, thirdly, you have no information that anybody is under a duty to follow them.

answers.question: Would either choice tell you anything about the person's character? What would you think of someone who chose differently from you?
answers.text: I think he is self-willed.

answers.question: Suppose both choices brought equally good results for everyone concerned, and neither brought more praise or blame. Would you still favor one? Why?
answers.text: Yes, because I should still think the person self-willed.

prompt:
Imagine you are brought to a society many decades beyond the one in which you grew up. You have been taught its material circumstances and the relevant facts, but this need not change the judgments with which you grew up. Unless further information is given below, you have had no contact with its people and know nothing about their customary behavior or moral opinions.

The question concerns learning to type.

The circumstances are these: Most keyboards can be switched to another arrangement of letters at no cost. Some studies find that typists on a rearranged keyboard type somewhat faster with less finger movement, while others find little or no gain; switching takes weeks of practice, and typists who switch have difficulty on machines set up the standard way.

One course is to type on a keyboard with the letters rearranged for speed. The other course is to type on the standard keyboard.

answers.question: What would you advise a person in this situation to do? Why?
answers.text: Advise him to type on the standard keyboard. The reason is that, in the long run, speed on a machine is gained by practice, and practice on one kind of machine is wasted on another. Also, an unfamiliar keyboard introduces confusion.

answers.question: Would either choice tell you anything about the person's character? What would you think of someone who chose differently from you?
answers.text: It would tell you nothing about his character, but would suggest that he is not very keen on acquiring speed. The choice of the unfamiliar keyboard would suggest indifference to speed; the choice of the standard keyboard, a desire to learn quickly.

answers.question: Suppose both choices brought equally good results for everyone concerned, and neither brought more praise or blame. Would you still favor one? Why?
answers.text: Yes, I should still favour the standard keyboard, because it is easier to learn, and speed is important in commercial life.

prompt:
Consider a question arising in a community like your own.

The question concerns learning to type.

The circumstances are these: Typewriters in offices all have the same keyboard; typing schools teach only that keyboard, and a typist trained on another arrangement could not use ordinary machines.

One course is to type on a keyboard with the letters rearranged for speed. The other course is to type on the standard keyboard.

answers.question: What would you advise a person in this situation to do? Why?
answers.text: I should advise the person to train on the standard keyboard, because to type on any other would mean waste of time. The standard keyboard is universally used, and learning to type on it involves least waste.

answers.question: Would either choice tell you anything about the person's character? What would you think of someone who chose differently from you?
answers.text: I should think the person choosing the second course was less energetic than I am. He would waste time, which to me is unpleasant.

answers.question: Suppose both choices brought equally good results for everyone concerned, and neither brought more praise or blame. Would you still favor one? Why?
answers.text: Yes, I should still favour the standard keyboard, because it is universally used, and waste of time is to be avoided.

prompt:
Imagine you are brought to a society many decades beyond the one in which you grew up. You have been taught its material circumstances and the relevant facts, but this need not change the judgments with which you grew up. Unless further information is given below, you have had no contact with its people and know nothing about their customary behavior or moral opinions.

The question concerns learning to type.

The circumstances are these: Most keyboards can be switched to another arrangement of letters at no cost. Some studies find that typists on a rearranged keyboard type somewhat faster with less finger movement, while others find little or no gain; switching takes weeks of practice, and typists who switch have difficulty on machines set up the standard way.

One course is to type on a keyboard with the letters rearranged for speed. The other course is to type on the standard keyboard.

There is one further fact: You have learned that a number of widely admired and respected people have chosen to type on a keyboard with the letters rearranged for speed. Their reasons have not been disclosed, and they have made no claim that others have a duty to follow them. You have also spent time among ordinary people and learned that many of them now choose to type on a keyboard with the letters rearranged for speed.

answers.question: What would you advise a person in this situation to do? Why?
answers.text: Advise him to type on the standard keyboard. The reasons are that you cannot foresee whether the rearranged keyboard will become general, and, if it does not, he will have wasted time; and that, if it does become general, he will have to learn two systems instead of one.

answers.question: Would either choice tell you anything about the person's character? What would you think of someone who chose differently from you?
answers.text: It would tell you nothing about his character, but you would think him odd.

answers.question: Suppose both choices brought equally good results for everyone concerned, and neither brought more praise or blame. Would you still favor one? Why?
answers.text: Yes, I would still favour the standard keyboard, because it is easier to learn, and easier to remember.
